title: Ohm's Law and Power
subject: Circuit Fundamentals
blurb: One relationship between four quantities, seen from every corner. Where it holds, where it quietly fails, and why I²R is the term that burns things.

slides.title:
Ohm's Law
and Power
slides.lead: Four quantities, one relationship. Fix any two and the other two are already decided.

slides.title:
Twelve formulas,
or one idea
slides.lead: Most courses hand out a wheel of twelve rearrangements and expect you to memorise it. There is nothing to memorise. There are two relationships, and everything on that wheel is algebra applied to them.

columns.label: What the wheel gives you
items: Twelve formulas that all look equally important
No sense of which one to reach for
Nothing about when any of it stops being true
A memory problem instead of an understanding problem

columns.label: What you actually need
items: V = IR, and P = VI
Any two of V, I, R, P fix the other two
The rest is substitution
Plus one thing the wheel never tells you

slides.callout: That last point is most of this volt. The wheel is true, and it is not the interesting part.

slides.title:
Pressure, flow,
and something in the way

points.text: Voltage is pressure difference. It is always measured between two points. A single point has no voltage, the same way a single spot in a pipe has no pressure difference.
Current is flow rate. Charge per second past a point, measured in amperes. Flow is the same everywhere along one unbranched pipe.
Resistance is restriction. A narrow section. More restriction means less flow for the same pressure.
Then stop using it. Water does not model capacitance, inductance, or anything non-linear. It gets you to V = IR and no further.

slides.callout: Every analogy has a range of validity. This one ends about four slides from here, and it is worth knowing that before you lean on it.

slides.title: V = IR, three ways
slides.lead: One equation, rearranged. Which form you write down depends only on which quantity you do not yet know.

formulas.label: Solve for voltage
formulas.note: You know the current through a component and its resistance. This gives the voltage dropped across it. The most common form in analysis.

formulas.label: Solve for current
formulas.note: You know the voltage across a component. This gives the current that will flow. The most common form in design, because supply voltage is usually the fixed quantity.

points.text: Solve for resistance: R = V / I. Rarely used to design something — mostly used to measure or to check a suspicion about a part.
Watch the units. Volts, amperes, ohms. Milliamps and kilohms cancel to volts, which is convenient and also the single most common place to lose a factor of a thousand.

slides.title:
Ohm's law is not
a law of nature

points.text: It is a property some materials happen to have. Metals at constant temperature obey it well. Nothing guarantees anything else will.
A device that obeys it is called ohmic. On a current-versus-voltage plot it draws a straight line through the origin. Nothing else does.
The slope of that line is 1/R. Steeper line, less resistance. Drag the resistance and watch the line pivot about the origin.
Resistance is the whole line, not one point. That distinction looks pedantic here and matters enormously on the next slide.

slides.title:
Put a diode on
the same axes

points.text: The line becomes a curve. Almost no current below about 0.6 V, then current rises very steeply. Switch the device selector and compare.
So what is its resistance? V/I gives a different answer at every point on the curve. The question has no single answer.
Engineers answer it two ways. V/I at one operating point is the DC resistance. The local slope there is the dynamic resistance. They are different numbers.
Lamps, thermistors, transistors, LEDs. All non-ohmic. Ohmic components are a special case you happen to meet first.

slides.callout: This is why the wheel is dangerous on its own: every formula on it silently assumes R is a constant.

slides.title:
Power is the rate
energy is delivered
slides.lead: Voltage and current describe what the electricity is doing. Power describes what it costs, how hot the part gets, and how big the heatsink has to be. P = VI, measured in watts, which is joules per second.

columns.label: Energy
items: Measured in joules, or watt-hours
A total — how much was delivered
What a battery stores and an electricity bill charges for
Depends on how long you ran for

columns.label: Power
items: Measured in watts
A rate — how fast it is being delivered
What sets the temperature of a component
Independent of how long you ran for

slides.callout: Components are rated in watts, not joules. A resistor does not care how long you leave it on — it cares how fast it has to shed heat.

slides.title:
Substitute Ohm's law
into P = VI
slides.lead: The two extra forms are not new physics. They are P = VI with V or I eliminated using V = IR. Reach for whichever form matches the two quantities you already know.

formulas.label: When you know current
formulas.note: Substituted V = IR. Use this for anything carrying a known current: wiring, shunts, MOSFETs while conducting, transformer windings.

formulas.label: When you know voltage
formulas.note: Substituted I = V/R. Use this for anything sitting across a known voltage: a pull-up, a bleeder resistor, a load on a fixed supply.

points.text: All three are the same statement. P = VI, P = I²R, P = V²/R. Which one saves you an algebra step depends on what you measured.
Both substitutions assume R is constant. On a diode or a lamp, only P = VI survives.

slides.title:
Double the current,
quadruple the heat

points.text: The square is the whole story. Power in a fixed resistance scales with the square of current. Drag the slider and watch the dissipation curve away from the current.
A 20% current margin is a 44% power margin. This is why current headroom disappears faster than engineers expect.
It runs away. Most conductors gain resistance as they heat, which raises I²R, which heats them further. Copper gains roughly 0.4% per °C.
Nearly every thermal problem is this term. Wire gauge, fuse ratings, trace widths, connector selection — all of it is I²R.

slides.title:
Why power lines
run at 400,000 volts

points.text: Deliver 100 MW down a line of 5 Ω. The power delivered is fixed by the customer. The voltage you send it at is your choice.
At 10 kV: I = 10 kA, so loss = I²R = 500 MW. You would need to generate six times what you deliver. Impossible.
At 400 kV: I = 250 A, so loss = 313 kW. Around 0.3% of what you sent.
40× the voltage, 1600× less loss. The entire high-voltage grid exists because of the square in I²R. Transformers exist to make this trade available.

slides.title:
The quarter-watt part
that smokes

points.text: A 220 Ω resistor across 12 V. I = 12/220 = 55 mA. P = V²/R = 144/220 = 0.65 W.
A standard through-hole resistor is rated 0.25 W. You are asking it to dissipate more than twice that. It will discolour, drift, then fail.
The resistance was never wrong. The circuit works exactly as calculated — right up until the part cooks. Ohm's law said nothing about this.
Derate. Pick a part rated at roughly twice the calculated dissipation. Here that means a 2 W resistor, or a different circuit.

slides.callout: Every component has a rating that lives outside Ohm's law. Checking it is a separate step, and it is the step beginners skip.

points.text: V, I, R and P are one system with two degrees of freedom. Set any two and the remaining two are already determined. Try any pair in the solver.
This is what the wheel was trying to say. Twelve formulas, six pairs, one relationship. Nothing to memorise.
In practice two are usually given to you. The supply fixes V. The datasheet fixes R, or the load fixes P. You solve for what is left.
And it all rests on R being constant. Which, four slides ago, we established is a special case.

slides.title:
Four ways this
goes wrong
slides.lead: None of these are failures of the equation. They are failures to notice what the equation assumes.

columns.label: Arithmetic and units
items: Kilohms and milliamps left unconverted — a factor of 1000
Voltage read as absolute rather than as a difference between two nodes
Reading the ohms wheel's P = V²/R and forgetting V is the drop across that part, not the supply

columns.label: Assumptions
items: Treating R as constant when the part is heating
Applying V = IR to a diode, an LED, or a lamp
Sizing a resistor for resistance and never checking its power rating

slides.callout: If a circuit behaves as calculated at first and drifts after a minute, suspect temperature before you suspect your algebra.

slides.title:
What you can
now do
slides.lead: The wheel is now a consequence rather than a thing to memorise, and you know the boundary of where it applies.

columns.label: You can now
items: Solve for any of V, I, R, P given any two
Read an I–V curve and say whether a device is ohmic
Size a resistor for power as well as resistance
Explain why the grid runs at high voltage
